items.title: Clinical terms and causes
items.text:
CLINICAL TERMS
Hepatitis: inflammation of liver.
Acute hepatitis: symptoms last less than 6 months.
Acute hepatic failure: a rapid deterioration of severe complications after the first signs of liver disease, such as jaundice, indicating sustained severe liver damage (loss of function of 80–90% of liver cells). Massive hepatic necrosis with impaired consciousness occurs within 8 weeks of onset.
Chronic hepatitis: inflammation of liver for at least 6 months.
Cirrhosis: replacement of liver tissue by fibrosis (scar tissue), leading to loss of liver function.
Fulminant hepatitis: severe impairment of hepatic function or severe necrosis of hepatocytes in the absence of pre-existing liver disease.
ACUTE HEPATITIS — CAUSES
Infectious: viral hepatitis A, B, C, D, E; less commonly HSV, CMV, EBV and yellow fever virus; non-viral malaria, brucellosis and leptospirosis.
Non-infectious: drugs (halothane, paracetamol/Tylenol, INH, alcohol, DDT); toxins (Jamaica bush tea, mushroom); vascular (hypotension and Budd–Chiari syndrome); autoimmune hepatitis; metabolic causes (Wilson disease and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency).
CHRONIC HEPATITIS — CAUSES
Viral hepatitis B and C; drugs (methotrexate, amiodarone, INH); alcohol; NAFLD; autoimmune causes (AIH, PBC, PSC); metabolic causes (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease).

items.title: Acute viral hepatitis comparison and Hepatitis A
items.text:
Acute viral hepatitis is a systemic disease with primary inflammation of the liver caused by a heterogeneous group of hepatotropic viruses.
ETIOLOGY SUMMARY
Hepatitis A: enterovirus, RNA; fecal–oral transmission; incubation 2–6 weeks; sporadic or epidemic; children or young adults; usually mild; no chronicity; prophylaxis with immunoglobulin and vaccine.
Hepatitis B: hepadnavirus, DNA; parenteral (blood/needles), sexual and vertical transmission; incubation 1–6 months; sporadic; any age; severe acute infection; chronicity; prophylaxis with immunoglobulin and vaccine.
Hepatitis C: flavivirus, RNA; parenteral transmission; incubation 1–6 months; sporadic; any age; usually mild acute infection; chronicity; no specific prophylaxis listed.
Hepatitis D: incomplete virus, RNA; parenteral transmission; incubation 1–6 months; sporadic; any age; severe acute infection; HBV vaccine provides prevention by preventing HBV.
Hepatitis E: calicivirus, RNA; fecal–oral transmission; incubation 2–6 weeks; sporadic or epidemic; children or young adults; usually mild except in pregnant females; no chronicity in the lecture comparison.
HEPATITIS A
An acute infectious disease caused by hepatitis A virus (HAV), formerly called infectious hepatitis or epidemic jaundice.
Agent: enterovirus of the Picornaviridae family; multiplies only in hepatocytes.
Resistance: fairly resistant to heat and chemicals; virus is highly susceptible to chlorine in usual doses; formalin is used to disinfect infected stools; inactivated by ultraviolet rays and by boiling for 5 minutes or autoclaving.
Virus excretion: infectivity from 2 weeks before to 1–2 weeks after onset of jaundice.

items.title: HAV host factors and HBV agent
items.text:
HEPATITIS A — HOST AND ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS
Age: HAV is more frequent among children than adults, but people of any age may be infected if susceptible.
Sex: both sexes are equally susceptible.
Immunity: immunity after attack probably lasts for life.
Environmental factors: cases may occur throughout the year.
Incubation: 10–50 days, usually 25–30 days.
Mode of transmission: fecal–oral route is the major route, including contaminated water, food or milk.
HEPATITIS B
An acute systemic infection with major pathology in the liver caused by hepatitis B virus; endemic throughout the world, especially in tropical and developing countries.
Agent: HBV, a 42 nm double-shelled DNA virus originally known as the Dane particle. It replicates in liver cells.
Morphology in serum: small spherical particles (~22 nm), filamentous or tubular particles (20–22 nm diameter), and Dane particles. Only the Dane particle is considered infectious.
Infective material: contaminated blood is the main source; virus has also been found in saliva, vaginal secretion and semen.
Resistance: readily destroyed by sodium hypochlorite or heat sterilization in an autoclave for 30–60 minutes.

items.title: HBV host factors, risk groups and transmission
items.text:
HEPATITIS B — AGE AND CHRONICITY
Acute hepatitis B: approximately 90% resolve by themselves; less than 1% develop fulminant hepatic failure. It occurs in approximately 1% of perinatal infection, over 10% of childhood infection (1–5 years), and over 30% after 5 years of age.
Chronic hepatitis B: approximately 2–10% progress to chronic state overall; about 95% after perinatal infection, over 80% after childhood infection, and 5–10% after age 5.
The lecture notes state that acute hepatitis B becomes chronic in over 90% of infants, 25–50% of children aged 1–5 years, and under 5% of older children and adults. Immunosuppressed patients, including those with HIV or on hemodialysis, have increased risk of chronic infection.
RESPONSIBLE POPULATION
Parenteral drug abusers; hemophilia and hemolytic anemia patients; homosexuals and people with multiple sexual partners; health-care professionals; babies born to mothers with positive HBsAg; and people living in high-prevalence areas.
ANTIGENS AND ANTIBODY RESPONSE
HBsAg (Australian antigen), HBcAg (core antigen) and HBeAg (envelope antigen) stimulate production of corresponding antibodies.
Incubation: 45–180 days, usually 60–90 days.
Transmission: parenteral, sexual and perinatal/vertical. Perinatal transmission is the main means of transmission in high-prevalence populations, especially from HBeAg-positive mothers.

items.title: Hepatitis C and D
items.text:
HEPATITIS C
An estimated 150–200 million people, or 3% of the world population, live with chronic hepatitis C. Seven major genotypes have been identified; genotype 4 is the most common variant in Egypt. Approximately 50–80% of infected patients progress to chronic hepatitis.
Agent: HCV, a Flaviviridae virus with a 50–60 nm virion, linear single-stranded RNA genome, core and lipid envelope. The half-life of the virus particles in serum is around 3 hours and may be as short as 45 minutes. The virus replicates in the liver and can multiply in lymphocytes.
Incubation: 40–120 days.
Transmission: mainly parenteral. Risk includes IV drug use, health-care work, transfusion of blood products, organ transplantation without screening, hemodialysis and accidental needle-stick injuries. Sexual transmission is associated with multiple partners and certain exposure patterns. Perinatal transmission may occur.
HEPATITIS D
HDV is a subviral satellite requiring hepatitis B virus to propagate. It may occur as superinfection in a chronic HBV carrier or as coinfection with HBV, which can result in severe acute infection.
Virus: spherical, 36–38 nm particle with an outer coat composed of HBsAg surrounding an ssRNA genome.
Incubation: 2–12 weeks.
Transmission: primarily parenteral and believed to be similar to HBV; the lecture notes state that HDV does not appear to be sexually transmitted.

items.title: Hepatitis E and G
items.text:
HEPATITIS E
Often causes an acute, self-limiting infection, but immunocompromised patients—particularly solid-organ transplant recipients—may develop chronic hepatitis with substantial mortality. In pregnant women, disease is more often severe and associated with a clinical syndrome called fulminant hepatic failure.
Agent: classified in the genus Herpes virus under the family Caliciviridae in the lecture source; a spherical, non-enveloped virus 29–32 nm in diameter with an ssRNA genome. The surface has virion projections and the virus is very labile.
Animal reservoir: pigs.
Incubation: 3–8 weeks.
Transmission: mainly fecal–oral, including fecal contamination of water or food; person-to-person transmission is uncommon.
HEPATITIS G
GB virus C (GBV-C), formerly hepatitis G virus (HGV) and also known as HpgV, is a Flaviviridae virus and is not known to cause human disease. HGV RNA has been found in patients with acute, chronic and fulminant hepatitis, hemophilia, multiple transfusions, hemodialysis, IV drug use and blood donation.

items.title: Pathology and clinical course
items.text:
PATHOLOGY
Centrilobular (zone 3) hepatic necrosis with diffuse infiltration by mononuclear cells (lymphocytes and plasma cells); histiocytes together with Kupffer-cell hyperplasia. In severe and fulminant cases, there is massive necrosis with marked reduction of liver size. Virus may affect kidney, synovial membranes and other sites.
CLINICAL PICTURE
Patients may be asymptomatic, have anicteric hepatitis, icteric hepatitis or complications.
Anicteric hepatitis is non-specific and may resemble influenza or typhoid; jaundice is absent, so diagnosis may be missed.
ICTERIC HEPATITIS — THREE STAGES
1. Pre-icteric stage: fever, malaise, headache, nausea and vomiting, anorexia—especially to cigarettes and meat—and headache that may be severe, especially in children, with or without photophobia. Pain in the right hypochondrium and epigastrium. Signs include fever with relative bradycardia, enlarged tender liver, and in some patients non-specific abdominal rash.
2. Icteric stage: anorexia improves and fever drops; jaundice appears with dark urine and pale stool. Temperature is normal; the liver is enlarged and tender; splenomegaly occurs in about 20% and cervical lymph nodes in about 10%.
3. Convalescent stage: gradual improvement in symptoms and signs. The liver returns to normal within 6 months. Complete recovery occurs in most HAV and HEV cases.

items.title: Complications and investigations
items.text:
COMPLICATIONS
Hepatic: relapse (clinical or biochemical); fulminant hepatic failure—massive hepatic necrosis may occur with HBV and HDV but is rare with HAV and HEV, except in pregnancy; post-hepatitic cholestasis (Watson syndrome) with jaundice and pruritus for 8–28 weeks due to hepatocyte edema, followed by complete recovery and more common in HAV; post-hepatitis syndrome (transaminitis) with anxiety and inadequate understanding; chronic complications—carrier state, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma—do not occur with HAV or HEV in this lecture.
Extrahepatic: immunological reactions to HBV or HCV may include arthritis, PAN, glomerulonephritis, aplastic anemia, cryoglobulinemia and Guillain–Barré syndrome.
INVESTIGATIONS
Liver enzymes and function: ALT and AST increased in hundreds; bilirubin increased, both direct and indirect; alkaline phosphatase increased; plasma proteins show elevated globulins with normal albumin.
Urine: bilirubin appears early; bile salts may be present.
Stool: pale and may show steatorrhea; diminished stercobilin.
Blood: ESR increased; leukopenia with relative lymphocytosis.

items.title: Viral markers
items.text:
HEPATITIS A MARKERS
Anti-HAV antibodies by ELISA: IgM denotes acute infection; IgG denotes old infection. Other methods listed are virus isolation, demonstration of virus in feces/blood/bile by immunoelectron microscopy, and RT-PCR of feces.
HEPATITIS B MARKERS
HBsAg is the first marker to appear in blood, around 6 weeks after infection, and disappears in about 3 months. Persistence denotes carrier or chronic state.
Anti-HBs appears after about 3 months; disappearance of HBsAg with appearance of anti-HBs signals recovery and non-infectivity.
HBcAg is detected in liver biopsy, not blood.
Anti-HBc IgM appears shortly after HBsAg, may persist for 3–6 months or longer and indicates active hepatitis. Anti-HBc IgG appears during acute HBV but persists indefinitely, denoting old infection or chronic carrier state.
HBeAg appears with or soon after HBsAg, indicates viral replication and infectivity, and persistence beyond 3 months indicates increased likelihood of chronic hepatitis B. The lecture notes state that HBeAg negativity may indicate the wild strain. Anti-HBe indicates low infectivity. PCR for HBV DNA is the most accurate method for detecting viral replication.
Liver biopsy with histology and immunoperoxidase staining may determine grade (inflammation) and stage (fibrosis) in chronic hepatitis.
HDV: delta antigen in liver-cell nuclei by immunofluorescence; anti-delta antibodies by ELISA. IgM appears 2–3 weeks after infection and is soon replaced by IgG in acute delta infection.
HCV: anti-HCV by ELISA is not useful in the early acute phase because antibodies take at least 4 weeks; HCV RNA by PCR or branched DNA can diagnose acute infection and monitor response; HCV antigen EIA may be used similarly and is easier to perform.
HEV: anti-HEV IgM and IgG.

items.title: Treatment and prophylaxis
items.text:
GENERAL TREATMENT
Rest until symptoms resolve, liver tenderness disappears and serum bilirubin is below 1.5 mg/dL. Carbohydrates and proteins are given freely; protein is restricted only in hepatic failure. Fats may worsen nausea and are better avoided. Symptomatic treatment includes domperidone for nausea/vomiting and cholestyramine for itching. Prophylaxis includes hygienic measures, immunoglobulins and vaccines.
HAV PROPHYLAXIS
Pre-exposure HAV vaccine: for travelers to endemic areas, given 4 weeks before travel; the lecture states 100% protection for more than 10 years. Immunoglobulin is used when there is allergy to a vaccine component and gives protection for 2–6 months.
Post-exposure immunoglobulin: within 2 weeks of exposure in an unvaccinated individual; vaccine may be given at the same time in a different limb.
HBV PROPHYLAXIS
Pre-exposure vaccine for high-risk individuals; prevaccination screening helps avoid vaccinating those with chronic infection. Dosing at 0, 1 and 6 months. Booster or revaccination for non-responders with anti-HBs below 10 mIU/mL.
Post-exposure HBIG: for children born to HBV-positive mothers and needle-stick injury. HBIG should be given within 48 hours, with the first HBV vaccine dose at a different body site.
National immunization schedule shown in the lecture: hepatitis B at birth or as soon as possible within 24 hours, 0.5 mL IM in the anterolateral mid-thigh; subsequent hepatitis B-containing doses at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, 0.5 mL IM in the anterolateral mid-thigh. Other measures include screening blood donors and blood/body-fluid precautions.
HCV
The lecture describes older peginterferon-based treatment for acute hepatitis C and notes that oral direct-acting agents have supplanted interferon therapy; a 6-week course of ledipasvir and sofosbuvir is stated to prevent chronic hepatitis.

Autoimmune Hepatitis
Liver Diseases
1. Definition
Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is a chronic, unresolving, severe inflammation of the liver resulting from a
complex interaction between triggering environmental factors, autoantigens, and genetic predisposition,
leading to a dysregulated immunoregulatory network.
Defining Characteristics
› Interface hepatitis with portal plasma cell infiltration (hallmark histological finding)
› Hypergammaglobulinemia and presence of circulating autoantibodies
› Continuing / unresolving hepatocellular inflammation and necrosis
› Progressive course — can advance to cirrhosis if untreated

items.text:
DISEASES OF THE PANCREAS
Pancreas Anatomy
✓ The pancreas is an elongated, tapered organ located across the back of the abdomen, behind
the stomach.
✓ The right side of the organ (called the head) is the widest part of the organ and lies in the
curve of the duodenum.
✓ The tapered left side extends slightly upward (called the body of the pancreas) and ends near
the spleen (called the tail)
✓ The pancreas is made up of two types of tissue:
▪ Exocrine tissue
The exocrine tissue secretes digestive enzymes. These are secreted into a network
of ducts that join the main pancreatic duct, which runs the length of the pancreas.
▪ Endocrine tissue
The endocrine tissue, which consists of the islets of Langerhans, secretes
hormones into the bloodstream.

items.title: ✓ The pancreas has digestive and hormonal functions:
items.breadcrumb: University Source › Diseases of the Pancreas
items.text:
✓ The pancreas has digestive and hormonal functions:
• The enzymes secreted by the exocrine tissue in the pancreas help break down
carbohydrates, fats, and proteins in the duodenum → These enzymes travel down
the pancreatic duct into the bile duct in an inactive form → When they enter the
duodenum, they are activated.
• The exocrine tissue also secretes bicarbonate to neutralize stomach acid in the
duodenum.
✓ The hormones secreted by the endocrine tissue in the pancreas are
• Insulin, glucagon (which regulate the level of glucose in the blood),
• Somatostatin (which prevents the release of the other two hormones), and many
others

items.title: WHAT IS PANCREATITIS?
items.breadcrumb: University Source › Diseases of the Pancreas
items.text:
WHAT IS PANCREATITIS?
Pancreatitis is an inflammatory process in which pancreatic enzymes auto digest the gland
Normally, digestive enzymes do not become active until they reach the small intestine, where
they begin digesting food.
✓ But if these enzymes become active inside the pancreas, they start "digesting" the pancreas
itself
✓ The gland can sometimes heal without any impairment of function or any morphologic
changes.
o This process is known as acute pancreatitis.
o It can recur intermittently, contributing to the functional and morphologic loss of
the gland → Recurrent attacks are referred to as chronic pancreatitis.
✓ Acute pancreatitis occurs suddenly and lasts for a short period of time and usually resolves.
✓ Chronic pancreatitis does not resolve itself and results in a slow destruction of the pancreas.
Acute pancreatitis
Definition
• Acute inflammation resulting from intrapancreatic activation of digestive enzymes
TYPES:
1. Acute edematous pancreatitis:
The pancreatic inflammation and disease is mild & self-limited in most patients with
peripancreatic fat necrosis but sparing acinar cells.
2. Hemorrhagic or necrotizing pancreatitis:
The inflammation may be extensive & progressing to coagulation necrosis of the
gland & the surrounding tissues
Epidemiology
✓ About 80,000 cases occur in the United States each year; some 20 percent of them are
severe.
✓ Acute pancreatitis occurs more often in men than women.

items.text:
Diagnosis of Acute Pancreatitis: Clinical Guidelines
1. The Diagnostic Criteria
A definitive diagnosis is generally made when at least two of the following are present:
1. Clinical: Characteristic upper abdominal pain.
2. Biochemical: Serum amylase or lipase ≥ 3 times the upper limit of normal.
3. Radiological: Evidence of pancreatic swelling or necrosis on Ultrasound or CT.
2. Laboratory Investigations
Enzyme Profiles
• Serum Amylase: Rises rapidly but may return to normal within 24–48 hours.
o Clinical Pearl: Persistent elevation suggests pseudocyst formation.
o Pancreatic Ascites: Amylase will be present in peritoneal fluid.
• Serum Lipase: More specific than amylase. It remains elevated for up to 12 days, making
it the preferred marker for late presentations or chronic-on-acute episodes.
• Urinary Amylase/Creatinine Ratio: Useful if serum amylase has already normalized.
Metabolic & Hematologic Markers
• CBC: Expect Leukocytosis (WBC > 12,000) with a shift to segmented polymorphs.
• CRP: Used for serial assessment to monitor the severity and inflammatory response.
• Hyperglycemia: Occurs due to beta-cell injury within the pancreatic islets.
• KFTs and Electrolytes (Na, K, Cl, Ca, P, Mg): Expect significant disturbances due to "third
spacing" of fluids.
• Calcium & Magnesium: Often decreased; monitoring is vital for prognosis.
• Liver Function Tests (ALT, AST, Alk Phos, Bilirubin): Transiently elevated, especially if
the etiology is biliary (gallstones).

items.title: Management of Severe Acute Pancreatitis
items.breadcrumb: University Source › Diseases of the Pancreas
items.text:
Management of Severe Acute Pancreatitis
1. NPO (Nil Per Os) – Nothing by mouth. Provide parenteral nutrition.
2. Analgesia – Administer pethidine for pain control.
3. Fluid Resuscitation – Correct hypovolemia with normal saline and/or colloids.
4. Monitoring – Insert CVP line and urinary catheter to monitor shocked patients.
5. Oxygen Therapy – Administer O₂ for hypoxia.
6. Respiratory Support – ARDS may require ventilatory support.
7. Glycemic Control – Use insulin for hyperglycemia.
8. Calcium Supplementation – IV calcium if tetany occurs.
9. GI Decompression – Nasogastric aspiration for paralytic ileus.
10. Thromboembolism Prophylaxis – Low-dose SC heparin.
11. Biliary Obstruction – If cholangitis or jaundice present, perform urgent ERCP to
remove stones and drain biliary system.
12. Antibiotics – Administer prophylactic antibiotics as indicated.
TTT of complications:
1. Necrotizing pancreatitis or pancreatic abscess urgent surgical debridement of the
pancreas
2. Pancreatic pseudocysts drainage into stomach or duodenum
3. Pancreatic ascites is indication for distal pancreatectomy

1.
Normal anatomy and histology Gross anatomy Anatomical feature Source-supported detail Overview The oesophagus is a muscular tube extending from the pharynx to the stomach.
Length Adult length: 25 cm (10 inches).
Incisor-to-LOS distance Distance from the incisors to the lower oesophageal sphincter: 40 cm.
Upper oesophageal sphincter The proximal oesophageal region at the cricopharyngeus is the upper oesophageal sphincter.
Lower oesophageal sphincter The portion adjacent to the anatomical gastro-oesophageal junction is the lower oesophageal sphincter (cardiac sphincter).
Constrictions Major constrictions shown: pharyngo-oesophageal at 16 cm, thoracic (aortobronchial) at 23 cm, and diaphragmatic near 38 cm; the abdominal oesophagus and cardiac stomach begin near 40 cm.
Histology Histological feature Source-supported detail Lining Lining: stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium.
Wall layers Wall layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria (muscularis externa), and adventitia/serosa in the intra-abdominal part.
2.
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) Physiology and pathophysiology
Between swallows, oesophageal muscles are relaxed except at the sphincters.
The lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) usually remains closed and relaxes when swallowing is initiated.
Transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations (TLESRs) are physiological but occur more frequently in GORD.
A small amount of reflux is normal.
Sphincter pressure rises in response to increased intra-abdominal and intragastric pressures.
Anti-reflux mechanisms
Main mechanisms: peristalsis, the diaphragm, the LOS, the intra-abdominal oesophageal segment, the mucosal valve, and unimpeded gastric emptying.
The intra-abdominal oesophageal segment acts as a flap valve.
A mucosal rosette formed by gastric mucosal folds and contraction of the crural diaphragm at the LOS acts like a pinchcock and prevents acid reflux.
A large hiatus hernia can impair this mechanism.
Refluxate is normally cleared rapidly by secondary peristalsis, gravity, and salivary bicarbonate.
Factors associated with reflux
Pregnancy and obesity.
Fat, chocolate, coffee, alcohol, and large meals.
Cigarette smoking.
Drugs: calcium-channel blockers and nitrates.
Systemic sclerosis.
After treatment of achalasia.
Hiatus hernia.
Oesophageal mucosal defence Defence level Source-supported details Surface defence Surface defence: mucus and the unstirred water layer trap bicarbonate; buffering is weak compared with the stomach and duodenum.
Epithelial defence
Epithelial defence: the apical cell membrane and junctional complexes limit H+ diffusion into cells.
In oesophagitis, junctional complexes are damaged.
Postepithelial defence
Postepithelial defence: bicarbonate normally buffers acid in cells and intracellular spaces.
Hydrogen ions impair growth and replication of damaged cells.
Sensory mechanism and pain
Sensory mechanism: acid activates primary sensory neurons through vanilloid receptor 1 (VR1).
This can initiate inflammation and release pro-inflammatory substances, producing pain.

items.title: University Source · Passage 2
items.text:
Defence level Source-supported details
Pain may also result from contraction of longitudinal oesophageal muscle.
2.
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) — continued Clinical features Clinical domain Source-supported details Core symptoms and heartburn
The two principal clinical features are heartburn and regurgitation.
Heartburn is the major feature.
Heartburn is aggravated by bending, stooping, and lying down, which promote acid exposure.
Heartburn is relieved by oral antacids.
Patients may report pain after hot liquids or alcohol.
Correlation between heartburn and oesophagitis is poor.
Diagnostic difficulty and testing
Differentiating cardiac from oesophageal pain can be difficult.
A PPI trial is worthwhile; if symptoms persist, ambulatory pH and impedance monitoring should be performed.
Regurgitation and respiratory features
Regurgitation of food and acid occurs particularly when bending or lying flat.
Aspiration pneumonia is unusual without an accompanying stricture.
Cough and asthma can occur and may respond slowly to a PPI (1-4 months).
Alarm features and appearances
Alarm symptoms may indicate Barrett's oesophagus, oesophageal stricture, or oesophageal cancer.
Alarm symptoms: dysphagia, early satiety, GI bleeding, odynophagia, vomiting, unexplained weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, choking, and continual pain.
Endoscopic appearances shown include the gastro-oesophageal junction, an oesophageal ulcer, and streaking oesophagitis.
GORD pain versus cardiac ischaemia GORD pain Cardiac ischaemic pain
GORD pain is burning, worse on bending, stooping, or lying down, and seldom radiates to the arms.
GORD pain is worse with hot drinks or alcohol and is relieved by antacids.
Cardiac ischaemic pain is gripping or crushing, radiates to the neck or left arm, is worse with exercise, and is accompanied by dyspnoea.
Diagnosis and investigations Approach/test Role and source-supported findings Threshold or trace Clinical approach
A clinical diagnosis can be made.
Patients younger than 45 years without alarm signs, especially dysphagia, can initially be treated without investigations. — Endoscopy Endoscopy assesses oesophagitis and hiatus hernia. — Intraluminal monitoring
Intraluminal monitoring documents reflux.
Options include 24-hour luminal pH monitoring or impedance combined with manometry.
Monitoring is helpful when there is no response to PPI and should always confirm reflux before surgery.
Excessive reflux: pH <4 for >4% of the monitored time.
Illustrated trace: five reflux episodes with pH <4 occurred, but only three produced symptoms.
Treatment: lifestyle and procedures
Lose weight and raise the head end of the bed at night.
Avoid precipitating factors and use dietary measures.
Reduce alcohol and caffeine consumption and stop smoking.
Treatment categories: lifestyle modification, drugs, endoluminal gastroplication, and surgery.
Endoluminal gastroplication is an endoscopic procedure in which multiple plications or pleats are made below the gastro-oesophageal junction.
Surgery should not be performed for hiatus hernia alone.
The best surgical predictor is typical reflux symptoms with documented acid reflux.
Surgical technique: return the oesophageal junction to the abdominal cavity, mobilize the gastric fundus, close the diaphragmatic crura snugly, and create a short tension-free fundoplication.
Indications are not clear; considerations include intolerance to medication, desire for freedom from medication, treatment expense, and concern about long-term adverse effects.
Patients with oesophageal dysmotility unrelated to acid reflux, no response to PPIs, or underlying functional bowel disease should not have surgery.
Drug treatment Class Examples or dose Mechanism/use Cautions or outcome Overview Drug groups: alginate-containing antacids, dopamine-antagonist prokinetics, H2-receptor antagonists, proton-pump inhibitors, and the potassium-competitive acid blocker vonoprazan. — — Alginate-containing antacids Alginate-containing antacids: 10 mL three times daily; available over the counter.
Alginates form a gel or 'foam raft' with gastric contents to reduce reflux.
Magnesium-containing antacids tend to cause diarrhoea; aluminium-containing compounds cause constipation.

items.title: University Source · Passage 3
items.text:
Class Examples or dose Mechanism/use Cautions or outcome Dopamine-antagonist prokinetics Metoclopramide and domepridone are dopamine-antagonist prokinetics that enhance peristalsis and accelerate gastric emptying. — — H2-receptor antagonists H2-receptor antagonists: cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine, and nizatidine.
H2-receptor antagonists suppress acid, are used if antacids fail, and are often available over the counter. — Proton-pump inhibitors PPIs listed: omeprazole, rabeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, and esomeprazole.
PPIs inhibit gastric hydrogen/potassium ATPase and reduce gastric acid secretion by 90%.
PPIs are the drug of choice for all mild cases; most patients respond well.
Heartburn persists in 20-30%; severe symptoms require twice-daily dosing and prolonged treatment.
Vonoprazan Vonoprazan is reported to be more potent than PPIs. — — Patterns among patients with reflux symptoms Phenotype/group Source-supported pattern Erosive oesophagitis Erosive oesophagitis: 20-30%; hiatus hernia 70%; pH-positive 75%; PPI response 90%.
Non-erosive reflux disease (NERD) Normal endoscopy occurs in 60-70% and represents non-erosive reflux disease (NERD), associated in the diagram with younger patients, women, and hiatus hernia in 30%.
Barrett's oesophagus Barrett's oesophagus: 6-12%; hiatus hernia 95%; pH-positive 75%. pH-positive NERD Among pH-positive NERD cases (60%), TLESRs are present and there is some PPI response. pH-negative functional group Among pH-negative cases (60%), the diagram labels the disorder 'functional'.
Hypersensitive oesophagus Of the pH-negative group, 40% have a hypersensitive oesophagus to minor pH changes with symptom index positive and some PPI response.
Functional heartburn The remaining 60% have functional heartburn driven by non-acid stimuli with a low PPI response.
Complications Aspect Source-supported detail Major complications Major complications: peptic stricture and Barrett's oesophagus.
Peptic stricture: occurrence Peptic strictures are uncommon in the PPI era and usually occur in patients older than 60 years.
Presentation Presentation: intermittent dysphagia for solids that worsens gradually over a long period.
Mild disease Mild cases may respond to PPI alone.
Severe disease Severe cases require endoscopic dilatation and long-term PPI therapy.
3.
Hiatus hernia Definition and pathogenesis
Hiatus hernia is herniation or protrusion of part of the stomach through the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm.
Oesophageal hiatal hernia accounts for 98% of diaphragmatic hernias.
Congenital hiatal hernias occur in infants and children; many cases are acquired later in life.
Fewer than 10% of adults with a hiatal hernia are symptomatic, generally in association with other causes of LES incompetence.
Symptoms, including heartburn and regurgitation of gastric juice, resemble GORD.
The basic defect is failure of the diaphragmatic muscle fibres forming the oesophageal hiatus margin, due to congenital or acquired oesophageal shortening.
A congenitally short oesophagus accounts for a small proportion of cases.
Acquired causes include age-related muscle degeneration.
Acquired causes include raised intra-abdominal pressure, such as pregnancy or abdominal tumours.
Recurrent oesophageal regurgitation and spasm may cause inflammation, fibrosis, and oesophageal shortening.
Increased fatty tissue in obesity may reduce diaphragmatic muscular elasticity.
Anatomical patterns Type/frequency Anatomy GOJ/LOS position Clinical implication Sliding hernia
Sliding (oesophago-gastric) hernia is the commonest pattern (85%).
In a sliding hernia, the herniated stomach forms a supradiaphragmatic bell by sliding upward on both sides of the oesophagus.
In sliding hiatus hernia, the gastro-oesophageal junction and part of the stomach lie above the diaphragm.
Sliding hernia is present in 30% of people older than 50 years.
Sliding hernia produces no symptoms by itself; symptoms are due to reflux.

items.title: University Source · Passage 4
items.text:
Type/frequency Anatomy GOJ/LOS position Clinical implication Rolling hernia
Rolling (para-oesophageal) hernia occurs in 10%; the gastric cardia rolls upward beside the oesophagus into an intrathoracic sac.
In rolling hernia, part of the fundus prolapses through the hiatus alongside the oesophagus.
The LOS remains below the diaphragm and remains competent in rolling hernia.
Occasionally, severe pain occurs because of volvulus or strangulation.
Mixed hernia Mixed (transitional) hernia accounts for the remaining 5% and combines sliding and rolling components. — — 4.
Barrett's oesophagus Definition and diagnosis Aspect Source-supported detail Definition Normal squamous oesophageal epithelium is replaced by metaplastic columnar mucosa, forming a segment of columnar-lined oesophagus (CLO).
Associated anatomy A hiatus hernia is almost always present.
Endoscopy Endoscopy shows proximal displacement of the squamocolumnar mucosal junction.
Biopsy Biopsy demonstrates columnar lining above the proximal gastric folds.
Diagnostic wording According to the British Society of Gastroenterology wording on the slide, intestinal metaplasia is no longer required for diagnosis.
Illustrated appearances The endoscopic images contrast normal lower oesophagus with Barrett's mucosa and show proximal abnormal mucosal extension and a Barrett's lesion.
Morphology and risk Morphology or risk factor Source-supported detail Circumferential sheet Barrett's mucosa may appear as a continuous circumferential sheet.
Finger-like projections It may form finger-like projections extending upward from the squamocolumnar junction.
Mucosal islands It may form islands of columnar mucosa within residual squamous mucosa.
Central obesity Central obesity increases the risk of Barrett's oesophagus 4.3-fold.
Typical patient group It is commonest in middle-aged obese men.
Adenocarcinoma risk Oesophageal adenocarcinoma develops in 0.12-0.5%.
5.
Eosinophilic oesophagitis Domain Source-supported detail Trend Its incidence is increasing markedly.
Adult presentation Adults present with food impaction and dysphagia.
Child presentation Children present with feeding intolerance or GORD-like symptoms.
Histology The cardinal histological feature is epithelial infiltration by numerous eosinophils, especially superficially and at sites far from the gastro-oesophageal junction.
Distinction from other disease Eosinophil abundance helps distinguish the condition from GORD, Crohn disease, and other causes of oesophagitis.
Clinical clues Typical clinical clues include failure of high-dose PPI treatment and absence of acid reflux.
Atopic associations Most affected patients are atopic; associations include atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, asthma, and modest peripheral eosinophilia.
Treatment Treatment includes dietary restriction of food allergens such as cow's milk and soy products, plus topical or systemic corticosteroids.
6.
Achalasia of the cardia History
In 1913, Ernest Heller performed the first surgical intervention; the procedure still carries his name.
Arthur Hurst used the term achalasia in a 1927 article on the treatment of 'cardiospasm'.
Achalasia is Greek for 'lack of relaxation'.
Ellis and colleagues described the first transthoracic approach in 1958.
Sir Alfred Cuschieri performed the first laparoscopic Heller myotomy in 1991.

items.title: University Source · Passage 5
items.text:
Definition and histopathology Feature Source-supported detail Core definition Achalasia consists of aperistalsis of the oesophageal body and a hypertonic lower oesophageal sphincter.
Neuronal degeneration It results from degeneration of neurons in the oesophageal wall.
Relative frequency It is the second most common benign oesophageal disorder requiring surgical intervention.
Myenteric plexus Histology shows decreased neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus.
Nitric-oxide-producing cells Nitric-oxide-producing cells, which contribute to LES relaxation, are preferentially depleted.
Cholinergic neurons Cholinergic neurons that maintain LES tone are relatively spared.
Functional consequence Loss of inhibitory neurons raises resting LES tone and causes oesophageal aperistalsis.
Aetiology Category Associations or mechanism Important clue Primary/immune associations
Primary achalasia is considered idiopathic.
HLA DQw1 and anti-myenteric antibodies have been associated with achalasia, supporting a proposed autoimmune mechanism. — Reported viral associations
Associations with chronic herpes zoster or measles have been reported.
T-cell reactivity to HSV-1 has been reported, suggesting a possible HSV-1-related mechanism. — Secondary achalasia: Chagas disease
Secondary achalasia may result from Chagas disease, which occurs mainly in Central and South America.
Chagas disease is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, carried by Rhodnius prolixus; the accompanying images show the parasite and vector.
Infection causes loss of ganglion cells in Auerbach's plexus. — Malignancy mimic Malignancy must be excluded because it can mimic achalasia.
Features suggesting malignancy: symptoms for <6 months, onset after age 60, excessive weight loss, and difficulty passing the endoscope through the gastro-oesophageal junction.
Incidence and clinical manifestations Clinical aspect Source-supported detail Annual incidence Annual incidence: 1.6 per 100,000 people.
Study limitation The relative rarity of achalasia makes it difficult to study compared with more common diseases.
Demographics It affects men and women equally and usually occurs at 20-50 years of age.
Dysphagia Dysphagia is the commonest symptom: food in >90% and liquids in >80%.
Comparison with dysmotility Other oesophageal dysmotility disorders may cause dysphagia, but not as frequently as achalasia.
Other manifestations Other manifestations: mild weight loss (usually <10 kg), regurgitation, chest pain, globus sensation, and hiccups.
Diagnosis Investigation/domain Characteristic findings Protected numbers or qualification General diagnostic course
Symptom onset is slow and gradual; the average interval from symptom onset to diagnosis is >4 years.
Three core diagnostic tools: barium swallow, endoscopy, and manometry. — Barium swallow Barium swallow is an excellent diagnostic tool; the classic appearance is a dilated oesophagus tapering to a 'bird's beak'.
Reported diagnostic accuracy of barium swallow: 95% in one study.
Manometry
Manometry finding 3: oesophageal aperistalsis; a swallow may produce no contraction or simultaneous contractions.
Contractions are classically low-amplitude, but high-amplitude simultaneous contractions define 'vigorous' achalasia.
Manometry finding 1: elevated resting LES pressure, often >45 mmHg.
Manometry finding 2: incomplete LES relaxation; normal relaxation should fall to <8 mmHg, whereas relaxation after a swallow may be incomplete or absent in achalasia.
Endoscopy
All patients with suspected achalasia should undergo upper-GI endoscopy to exclude malignancy.
At endoscopy, the oesophagus is usually enlarged and may contain retained food.
The LES does not open spontaneously but can be traversed with gentle pressure. — Additional imaging CT or endoscopic ultrasound may help if another cause, such as malignancy, is suspected. —

items.title: University Source · Passage 6
items.text:
6.
Achalasia of the cardia — treatment Medical therapy Aspect Source-supported detail Drug and timing Calcium-channel blockers or nitrates are taken 10-30 minutes before meals.
Role and limitation They have moderate success but require perpetual use and are not recommended as first-line therapy.
Botulinum toxin (BOTOX) Aspect Source-supported detail Mechanism Botulinum neurotoxin type A inhibits acetylcholine release.
Intended balance Blocking presynaptic acetylcholine release in Auerbach's plexus is intended to restore neurotransmitter balance.
Delivery BOTOX is injected endoscopically into the LES.
Standard technique Standard technique: 1 mL (20-25 units BT/mL) into each of four quadrants about 1 cm above the Z-line.
Complications Complications: mediastinitis, oesophageal mucosal ulceration, and pneumothorax.
Outcome over time Symptomatic relief may reach 90% after a few months but falls to 50% or less at 1 year and continues to decline.
Recommended role Consensus in the lecture: reserve BOTOX for patients unfit for other interventions.
Pneumatic dilatation Aspect Source-supported detail Role Pneumatic dilatation is considered the most effective non-surgical treatment.
Technique The balloon is positioned across the LES using endoscopy and fluoroscopy.
Pressure Inflation pressure: 7-15 psi.
Observation Patients are usually observed for 6 hours and then discharged.
Predictors of success Best predictors of success: post-dilatation pressure (or the pre/post pressure difference) and older age.
Perforation risk The main concern is oesophageal perforation; reported rates range from 1.6% to about 10%, with one study reporting 21%.
Heller myotomy and fundoplication Domain Source-supported details Historical and current technique
Heller's original 1913 operation used an abdominal approach with anterior and posterior oesophagomyotomy.
Current surgery usually performs only an anterior myotomy through an abdominal or thoracic approach; laparoscopic and thoracoscopic approaches are described.
The thoracic approach has drawbacks.
Laparoscopic myotomy is considered the standard operation, with complication rates similar to open surgery but shorter hospital stay and recovery.
Operative questions and antireflux rationale
Key operative questions: whether to add fundoplication, which fundoplication, management of sigmoid oesophagus, myotomy length, and possible robotic benefit.
Without an antireflux procedure, 30% reported significant heartburn and objective pH/endoscopy evidence of reflux occurred in 60%.
The cited analysis recommends a concurrent antireflux procedure with laparoscopic Heller myotomy.
Dor versus Toupet
Dor fundoplication is an anterior 180-degree wrap.
Toupet fundoplication is a posterior 270-degree wrap.
The lecture reports no significant difference between Dor and Toupet for dysphagia, GORD, or PPI use.
At the time of the cited slide, no randomized controlled trial had compared Dor and Toupet.
Sigmoid oesophagus
Achalasic sigmoid oesophagus is markedly dilated, tortuous, and angulated.
It was previously thought to require oesophagectomy or at least preclude fundoplication.
Myotomy length and later reports
Commonly quoted myotomy length: 5 cm on the oesophagus plus 1 cm onto the cardia.
A 2007 retrospective review reported superior long-term efficacy with extended Heller myotomy plus Toupet fundoplication.
A 2006 report described robot-assisted laparoscopic Heller myotomy as safe and effective.
Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM)
POEM is a submucosal endoscopic oesophageal myotomy first presented in the lecture as a novel experimental approach (Endoscopy, 2007).
POEM is considered a form of NOTES.
The lecture identifies Dr Haruhiro Inoue as the leading expert and states that he had performed >100 procedures.

items.title: University Source · Passage 7
items.text:
Enter the submucosal space about 15 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction using an endoscope with a transparent cap.
Saline with indigo dye is used to create a tunnel extending to about 2 cm beyond the gastro-oesophageal junction.
Myotomy begins about 10 cm proximal to the gastro-oesophageal junction and continues to 2 cm beyond it.
Only inner circular fibres are divided; outer longitudinal fibres remain intact.
The endoscope is removed from the tunnel and the entry site is closed with endoscopic clips.
Treatment algorithm and summary Modality/domain Source-supported summary Medical therapy Medical nitrates/CCBs are used primarily in older patients who cannot undergo surgery.
BOTOX BOTOX injection is endoscopic, time-limited, and requires repeat injections.
Pneumatic dilatation
The algorithm reports good long-term outcome in 50% after pneumatic dilatation, lists advanced achalasia as a contraindication, and gives a 7% perforation rate.
Pneumatic dilatation is effective but carries a perforation risk.
Heller myotomy
Heller myotomy is presented as the primary treatment for most operable symptomatic patients; it is an extramucosal cardiomyotomy with good results in >85%.
The algorithm recommends laparoscopic Heller myotomy plus partial fundoplication to reduce reflux after myotomy.
Laparoscopic Heller myotomy has excellent results and should be accompanied by Dor or Toupet fundoplication, not Nissen.
The summary recommends myotomy of at least 5 cm on the oesophagus and 2 cm on the stomach, possibly longer.
Advanced disease Oesophagectomy may be required in very advanced cases with megaoesophagus.
Cancer surveillance The lecture states a 3-5% risk of squamous-cell carcinoma in achalasia; risk does not decrease after successful myotomy, so periodic oesophagoscopy is advised.
Core mechanism Overall mechanism: myenteric plexus disease causes high resting LES pressure and oesophageal aperistalsis.
Overall treatment positioning Medical therapy is ineffective; BOTOX is reserved for patients unable to undergo other interventions.
Future and POEM
The robot may have a future role.
POEM shows promise, but the lecture notes insufficient long-term results and comparative studies for definitive conclusions.

items.text:
1.
Introduction & Clinical Context The investigation of hepatobiliary disorders requires a logical, stepwise approach combining clinical presentation with laboratory, radiological, and histopathological evaluations.
In clinical practice, liver diseases usually manifest as acute hepatitis, chronic liver disease/cirrhosis, cholestasis (obstructive or hepatocellular), or incidental abnormalities discovered on routine screening.
Investigations are systematically designed to determine the presence of liver disease, classify the type of injury (hepatocellular vs. cholestatic), evaluate synthetic function, and identify the specific etiology.
2.
Laboratory Investigations: Liver Function Tests (LFTs) Standard "Liver Function Tests" is a broad term that includes enzymes reflecting hepatocyte integrity or biliary clearance, as well as true markers of hepatic synthetic capacity.
A.
Markers of Hepatocellular Injury (Aminotransferases) Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT): Primarily localized to the liver cytosol; highly specific for hepatic parenchymal injury.
Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST): Present in liver (cytosol and mitochondria), cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle, kidneys, and brain.
Less specific than ALT.
Clinical Interpretation of Aminotransferase Elevations: Marked elevation (>1000 U/L): Suggests acute ischemic injury (shock liver), acute viral hepatitis, or toxin/ drug-induced liver injury (e.g., acetaminophen toxicity).
Mild-to-moderate elevation (<300 U/L): Common in Chronic Hepatitis B/C, Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD/MASLD), and Alcoholic Liver Disease.
AST:ALT Ratio (De Ritis Ratio): An AST:ALT ratio > 2:1 is highly suggestive of alcoholic liver disease, driven by pyridoxal-5-phosphate deficiency in alcoholics which selectively suppresses ALT.
A ratio > 1 in chronic viral hepatitis suggests progression to cirrhosis.
B.
Markers of Cholestasis and Biliary Secretory Function Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP): Synthesized by canalicular membranes of hepatocytes and bone, placenta, and intestine.
To confirm hepatic origin, pair it with Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT) or fractionate isoenzymes.
Isolated high ALP with normal GGT points to bone pathology.
Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT): Highly sensitive for hepatobiliary disease but lacks specificity (induced by alcohol ingestion, phenytoin, and various microsomal-inducing drugs).
◦ ◦ ◦

items.title: University Source · Passage 2
items.text:
C.
True Markers of Hepatic Synthetic Capacity Serum Albumin: Synthesized exclusively by the liver.
Because it has a long half-life (~20 days), low serum albumin is characteristic of chronic liver disease (e.g., cirrhosis) or severe protein-losing states, rather than acute liver injury.
Prothrombin Time (PT) and INR: Measures the extrinsic clotting pathway dependent on factors I, II, V, VII, and X.
Factor VII has the shortest half-life (~6 hours), making PT/INR an excellent, highly sensitive indicator of acute hepatic synthetic failure (e.g., fulminant hepatic failure) as well as chronic dysfunction.
D.
Excretory Markers: Serum Bilirubin Unconjugated (Indirect) Bilirubinemia: Driven by overproduction (hemolysis) or impaired hepatic conjugation (e.g., Gilbert’s syndrome).
Conjugated (Direct) Bilirubinemia: Indicates parenchymal liver damage or biliary tree obstruction (cholestasis).
Direct bilirubin fraction > 50% confirms a conjugated pattern.
Diagnostic Pattern Typical LFT Profiles Common Differential Diagnoses Hepatocellular Disproportionate elevation of ALT & AST compared to ALP.
Bilirubin may be elevated.
Acute or Chronic Viral Hepatitis, Toxin/Drug injury, Autoimmune Hepatitis, Ischemic Liver Injury.
Cholestatic / Obstructive Disproportionate elevation of ALP & GGT compared to ALT & AST.
Marked Conjugated Bilirubinemia.
Choledocholithiasis, Pancreatic Malignancy, Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC), Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC).
Infiltrative Elevated ALP (often marked) with near-normal or mildly elevated aminotransferases and bilirubin.
Hepatic Granulomas (Sarcoidosis, TB), Metastatic Malignancies, Hepatic Abscesses.
4th Year Exam Note: Vitamin K vs.
Parenchymal Dysfunction To differentiate prolonged PT caused by prolonged biliary obstruction (impaired fat-soluble Vitamin K absorption due to lack of bile salts) from severe parenchymal failure, administer parenteral Vitamin K.
If PT normalizes or improves by >30% within 24–48 hours, the defect is obstructive/absorptive.
If it fails to correct, it indicates severe parenchymal synthetic failure.
3.
Etiological Investigations Once a pattern of liver injury is established, specific serological, immunological, and metabolic profiles are requested to ascertain the underlying etiology.
A.
Viral Hepatitis Serology Suspected VirusPrimary Screening Test Confirmatory / Supplementary Tests Hepatitis A (HAV)Anti-HAV IgM (indicates acute infection)Anti-HAV IgG (indicates immunity via past exposure or vaccination)

items.title: University Source · Passage 3
items.text:
Suspected VirusPrimary Screening Test Confirmatory / Supplementary Tests Hepatitis B (HBV)HBsAg (Current infection) Anti-HBc IgM (Acute window period marker) HBV DNA via PCR (Viral load) HBeAg / Anti-HBe (Replication status) Anti-HBs (Immunity) Hepatitis C (HCV)Anti-HCV Antibody HCV RNA via PCR (Confirms active replication vs. resolved infection) Hepatitis E (HEV)Anti-HEV IgM HEV RNA in blood/stool (used in immunosuppressed cases) B.
Autoimmune Liver Diseases Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH): Characterized by hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG) and positive autoantibodies: Type 1 AIH: Anti-Nuclear Antibody (ANA) and/or Anti-Smooth Muscle Antibody (ASMA).
Type 2 AIH: Anti-Liver Kidney Microsome type 1 (Anti-LKM-1) antibodies; typically seen in pediatric populations.
Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC): Chronic cholestatic disease destroying intrahepatic small bile ducts.
Screening marker of choice is Anti-Mitochondrial Antibody (AMA), highly sensitive and specific (>95%).
Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC): Fibrosing inflammation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, strongly linked to Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD/Ulcerative Colitis).
Associated with Perinuclear Anti- Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies (p-ANCA), though diagnosis depends primarily on imaging.
C.
Metabolic and Genetic Inquiries Hereditary Hemochromatosis: Screen via Transferrin Saturation (elevated, often >45-50%) and Serum Ferritin.
Confirmed via HFE gene mutation analysis (C282Y/H63D).
Wilson's Disease: Disorder of copper excretion, presenting with neuropsychiatric symptoms and liver disease in young patients.
Screen via reduced Serum Ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL) and elevated 24-hour Urinary Copper Excretion.
Slit-lamp exam reveals Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings.
Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (A1AT) Deficiency: Suspected in patients presenting with concomitant early-onset emphysema and liver cirrhosis.
Investigated via serum A1AT levels and Pi-phenotyping.
4.
Imaging Modalities A.
Transabdominal Ultrasonography (US) The indispensable first-line, non-invasive imaging modality for nearly all suspected liver diseases.
Evaluates liver size, echogenicity (e.g., diffusely increased echogenicity indicating "fatty liver" / steatosis), and surface contour (nodularity suggests cirrhosis).
Detects dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts to differentiate intrahepatic cholestasis from mechanical extrahepatic biliary obstruction.
Evaluates for ascites, splenomegaly, and portal vein patency/flow direction using Doppler imaging.
◦ ◦

items.title: University Source · Passage 4
items.text:
B.
Computed Tomography (CT) & Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) Contrast-Enhanced Multi-phase CT/MRI: Critical for characterizing focal liver lesions (e.g., Hemangioma, Adenoma, Focal Nodular Hyperplasia, and Hepatocellular Carcinoma [HCC]).
HCC demonstrates a classic dynamic pattern: arterial phase hyperenhancement followed by venous/delayed phase washout.
Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP): Non-invasive T2-weighted MRI protocol optimal for visualizing biliary tree anatomy.
It is the gold standard for diagnosing PSC, showing a classic "beaded appearance" of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.
C.
Non-Invasive Fibrosis Assessment: Transient Elastography (FibroScan) Measures liver stiffness by calculating the velocity of a low-frequency shear wave passing through the parenchyma.
It has largely replaced diagnostic liver biopsies for staging fibrosis in chronic hepatitis B and C and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).
5.
Endoscopic and Invasive Investigations A.
Upper Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (Esophagogastroduodenoscopy - EGD) Essential screening tool in patients diagnosed with cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
It aims to identify, grade, and prophylactically manage esophageal and gastric varices or portal hypertensive gastropathy to prevent catastrophic variceal hemorrhage.
B.
Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) An invasive endoscopic-radiological tool.
Due to procedural risks (e.g., post-ERCP pancreatitis, cholangitis), its role has evolved to be primarily therapeutic rather than purely diagnostic.
It is utilized for common bile duct stone extraction, sphincterotomy, and biliary stenting across malignant or benign strictures.
C.
Histopathological Investigation: Liver Biopsy Historically the absolute gold standard; currently reserved for cases where non-invasive testing yields ambiguous or conflicting results.
Indications: Staging and grading chronic viral hepatitis when non-invasive tools are unavailable; diagnosing seronegative autoimmune hepatitis; evaluating unexplained hepatomegaly or persistent abnormal LFTs.
Absolute Contraindications: Severe uncorrectable coagulopathy (INR > 1.5), profound thrombocytopenia (Platelets < 50,000/µL), suspected vascular tumors or echinococcal (hydatid) cysts, and uncooperative patients.
6.
Diagnostic Algorithm: Summary Framework Step 1: Identify clinical syndrome (Acute liver failure, Jaundice, or Incidental abnormal LFTs).
Step 2: Evaluate standard LFTs.
Categorize into Hepatocellular (ALT/AST dominant) or Cholestatic (ALP/ GGT dominant).
Confirm synthetic reserve using PT/INR and Albumin.
Step 3: Order first-line Abdominal Ultrasound alongside initial baseline serologies (Viral markers for hepatocellular; biliary evaluation for cholestasis).
Step 4: Advance to specific autoantibodies, metabolic screens, or specialized dynamic cross-sectional imaging (MRCP/CT) based on Step 2 and 3 results.

items.title: 1.3 Multi-Organ Crosstalk in NAFLD

1.3 Multi-Organ Crosstalk in NAFLD
Organs Involved in NAFLD Pathogenesis (Inter-Organ Crosstalk)
› Adipose tissue: excess free fatty acids (FFAs) released → hepatic lipotoxicity and inflammation
› Pancreas: beta-cell dysfunction and insulin hypersecretion → hyperinsulinemia
› Gut (microbiome): dysbiosis → increased intestinal permeability → bacterial endotoxin → hepatic
TLR4 activation → inflammation
› Liver: central target — steatosis, necroinflammation, fibrosis, and eventually cirrhosis/HCC
› Lipids accumulating in the liver induce hepatic insulin resistance and inflammation — key driver of
NASH
1.4 Lipids induce hepatic IR and inflammation

Screening · Incidence · Risk Groups
2.1 Prevalence & Burden

• NAFLD parallels the prevalence of Metabolic Syndrome (MetS) and its components, which also
increase the risk of more advanced disease
• Prevalence is rising in parallel with global obesity and T2DM epidemics
• NAFLD is also found in 7% of lean (normal-weight) individuals — screening must not be based on
BMI alone
2.2 Screening Recommendations
Who to Screen (EASL Guidelines)
› Screen all patients with insulin resistance (IR) and/or metabolic risk factors (obesity, MetS) →
evaluate for NAFLD
› Screen all individuals with steatosis for secondary causes including careful alcohol intake
assessment
› Screen all NAFLD patients for coexisting chronic liver diseases that may worsen liver injury
› Screen all individuals with steatosis for MetS features, independent of liver enzyme levels
› In obesity / MetS: NAFLD screening should be part of routine work-up
Why Community Screening is Limited
› High direct and indirect costs
› Low predictive value of available non-invasive tests
› Risks associated with liver biopsy (required to confirm NASH)
› Lack of approved specific pharmacological treatments
→ BUT: Diagnosing NASH is valuable — it identifies patients at risk of fibrosis progression,
cirrhosis, and HCC
03 Pathogenesis
Lifestyle · Metabolic Syndrome · Genetics · Multi-organ Crosstalk
3.1 Lifestyle & Diet (Western Diet Hypothesis)
Lifestyle Factor Mechanism / Role in NAFLD
High caloric intake Positive energy balance → adipose deposition → hepatic steatosis
Excess saturated fat Direct hepatotoxic lipotoxicity; promotes hepatic IR
High fructose intake De novo lipogenesis in the liver; drives NASH progression
Sedentary behaviour Reduces peripheral glucose utilisation and muscle insulin sensitivity

Strongest phenotype; major driver of IR; predicts advanced disease
Obesity (BMI / waist ↑)
especially in elderly

progression of NAFLD. Assessment of dietary and physical activity habits is part of A 1
evidence rec. grade
comprehensive NAFLD screening
3.2 Genetic Modifiers
• Several genetic modifiers of NAFLD have been identified
– A minority have been robustly validated
• PNPLA3 I148M and TM6SF2 E167K carriers have a higher liver fat content
– Increased risk of NASH
– NAFLD not systematically associated with features of IR
★ Recommendation: Genotyping may be considered in selected patients and B 2
clinical studies but is NOT recommended routinely evidence rec. grade

3.4 Natural history of NAFLD over 8–13 years
NAFLD Natural History at 8–13 Years (Key Numbers)
Transition Rate
Simple steatosis → NASH (F1–F2 fibrosis) 12–40%
NASH → Advanced fibrosis (F3) 5–10%
NASH → Cirrhosis (F4) 0–50% (variable by population)
Cirrhosis → HCC 1–8% per year
Cirrhosis → Liver-related death / LTx ~13%
3.5 Liver Biopsy
• Liver biopsy is essential for the diagnosis of NASH
– Clinical, biochemical or imaging measures cannot distinguish NASH from steatosis
• NAFL encompasses
– Steatosis alone plus ONE of lobular or portal inflammation OR ballooning
• NASH requires
– Steatosis AND
– Lobular or portal inflammation AND
– Ballooning
• NAS scoring indicates disease severity
★ Recommendation: NASH must be diagnosed by liver biopsy showing steatosis +
hepatocyte ballooning + lobular inflammation. No non-invasive method can replace A 1
evidence rec. grade
this for diagnostic certainty

items.text:
3.6 Role of non-invasive assessments
• Non-invasive markers should aim to:
– Identify the risk of NAFLD among individuals with increased metabolic risk in primary
care
– Identify those with a worse prognosis in secondary and tertiary care, E.g. severe NASH
– Monitor disease progression
– Predict response to therapeutic interventions
→ Achieving these aims could reduce the need for liver biopsy
3.7 Non-Invasive Assessment of Steatosis
• Steatosis should be documented whenever NAFLD is suspected
– Predicts future T2DM, cardiovascular events and arterial hypertension
– Quantification of fat content is of limited clinical relevance
• Except as a surrogate of treatment effectiveness
★ Recommendation: US is the preferred first-line diagnostic procedure for A 1
imaging of NAFLD, as it provides additional diagnostic information evidence rec. grade
Whenever imaging tools are not available or feasible serum biomarkers and scores
are an acceptable alternative for the diagnosis of steatosis
B 2
A quantitative estimation of liver fat can only be obtained by 1H-MRS. This technique
is of value in clinical trials and experimental studies, but is expensive and not A 1
recommended in the clinical setting

Why Fibrosis Assessment Is the Priority
› Fibrosis stage is the MOST IMPORTANT prognostic factor in NAFLD
› Correlates directly with liver-related outcomes (decompensation, HCC) and all-cause mortality
› Advanced fibrosis indicates thorough investigation

acceptable non-invasive procedures to identify those at low risk of advanced A 2

3.9 Potential algorithm for non-invasive assessment: prediction rules and
blood-based biomarkers
3.10 Non-invasive assessment of paediatric NAFLD
• NAFLD should always be suspected in obese children
– Exclude other causes
– Evaluate elevated aminotransferase levels and liver hyperechogenicity
• Due to the poor sensitivity in overweight/obese children, non-invasive markers
and imaging techniques are the first diagnostic step
★ Recommendation: In children, predictors of fibrosis, including elastometry, ARFI B 2
imaging and serum biomarkers might help reduce the number of biopsies evidence rec. grade
04 Metabolic Associations
MetS · Obesity · T2DM · HOMA-IR
• NAFLD is closely associated with:
– IR in the liver as well as adipose and muscle tissue
– MetS
• Three of: impaired fasting glucose or T2DM, hypertriglyceridaemia, low HDL-C,
increased waist circumference,† high blood pressure
• All components of MetS correlate with liver fat content:
• Evaluate risk of NAFLD in patients with MetS
• Evaluate MetS in patients with NAFLD

items.title: 05 Diagnosis & Evaluation
items.text:
05 Diagnosis & Evaluation
• Incidental discovery of steatosis indicates comprehensive evaluation
– Family and personal history of NAFLD-associated diseases
– Exclusion of secondary causes of steatosis
5.1 Initial Evaluation Protocol
Level Variable
Initial 1. Alcohol intake: <20 g/day (women), <30 g/day (men)
2. Personal and family history of diabetes, hypertension and CVD
3. BMI, waist circumference, change in body weight
4. Hepatitis B/hepatitis C virus infection
5. History of steatosis-associated drugs
6. Liver enzymes (ALT, AST, GGT)
7. Fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, OGTT, (fasting insulin [HOMA-IR])
8. Complete blood count
9. Serum total and HDL cholesterol, triacylglycerol, uric acid
10. Ultrasonography (if suspected for raised liver enzymes)
Extended 1. Ferritin and transferrin saturation
2. Tests for coeliac and thyroid diseases, polycystic ovary syndrome
3. Tests for rare liver diseases (Wilson, autoimmune disease, AATD)
5.2 Diagnostic Flowchart Summary
• Metabolic work-up must carefully assess all components of MetS
• Obesity/T2DM or raised liver enzymes in patients with metabolic risk factors should prompt non-
invasive screening to predict steatosis, NASH and fibrosis

items.title: 06 Natural History & Complications
items.text:
06 Natural History & Complications
Progression · CVD · HCC
• In general, NAFLD is a slowly progressive disease, both in adults and in children
6.1 Fibrosis Progression Rates
1 stage / 14 Cirrhosis age
1 stage / 7 yrs x2 faster ~20% of cases
yrs NASH Progression HTN: Doubles rate Rapid Progressors 8
NAFL Progression Paediatric NASH
★ Recommendation: NASH patients with fibrosis and hypertension should receive B 1
closer monitoring — arterial hypertension doubles the rate of fibrosis progression evidence rec. grade
• Pediatric NAFLD is of concern
– Potential for severe liver-related complications later in life
– NASH-related cirrhosis has been reported as early as 8 years of age
6.2 Cardiovascular Disease (CVD)
• Prevalence and incidence of CVD is HIGHER in NAFLD than in matched controls
→ Driven by the strong association between NAFLD and MetS components
• CVD is the leading cause of death in NAFLD — more common than liver-related death (except in
advanced fibrosis)
• CVD risk must be assessed in all NAFLD patients regardless of traditional risk factors
• CVD and metabolic risk factors are reported even in adolescents and children with NAFLD
★ Recommendation: Cardiovascular system screening is MANDATORY in all A 1
individuals with NAFLD — CV complications frequently dictate overall outcome evidence rec. grade

items.title: 6.3 Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)
items.text:
6.3 Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)
• NAFLD is a recognised independent risk factor for HCC, even in the pre-cirrhotic stage
• PNPLA3 rs738409 C>G gene polymorphism significantly increases HCC risk in NAFLD
• HCC surveillance in non-cirrhotic NAFLD is NOT yet considered cost-effective
• Large NAFLD population makes systematic HCC surveillance largely impracticable
Note on HCC Surveillance
› No formal recommendation on timing or cost-effectiveness of HCC surveillance in NAFLD can
currently be made
› Standard HCC surveillance (6-monthly USS ± AFP) applies to NAFLD patients who have reached
cirrhosis (F4)
› PNPLA3 polymorphism carriers may warrant enhanced surveillance — under study
07 Treatment
Lifestyle · Pharmacotherapy · Surgery · Liver Transplantation
• Epidemiology suggests a close relationship between an unhealthy lifestyle and NAFLD
7.1 Diet & Lifestyle Changes (Mandatory in ALL Patients)
Lifestyle is First-Line Treatment for Every Patient with NAFLD
› Modest weight loss reduces liver fat, improves hepatic IR, and produces NASH regression
› Weight loss of ≥7% body weight is associated with significant histological improvement
› A pragmatic, individually tailored approach: dietary restriction PLUS progressive aerobic
exercise/resistance training
› Patients without NASH or fibrosis: lifestyle counselling only — no pharmacotherapy
★ Recommendation: Structured programmes aimed at lifestyle changes towards C 2
healthy diet and habitual physical activity are advisable in NAFLD evidence rec. grade
Patients without NASH or fibrosis should receive counselling for healthy diet and
physical activity but no pharmacotherapy
B 2
In overweight/obese NAFLD, a 7–10% weight loss is the target of most lifestyle
interventions, and results in improvement of liver enzymes and histology
B 1
Dietary recommendations should consider energy restriction and exclusion of NAFLD-
promoting components (processed food, and food and beverages high in added
fructose). The macronutrient composition should be adjusted according to the
B 1
Mediterranean diet
Both aerobic exercise and resistance training effectively reduce liver fat. The choice
of training should be tailored based on patients’ preferences to be maintained in the B 2
long-term

7.2 Pharmacotherapy
Indications for Drug Treatment
› Progressive NASH
› Early-stage NASH with risk of fibrosis progression (age >50 yrs + T2DM + MetS + elevated ALT)
› Active NASH with high necroinflammatory activity
› Significant fibrosis: stage F2 and higher → preferred candidates
⚠ Critical Point — Current Pharmacotherapy Status
› NO drugs are specifically approved for NAFLD / NASH
› NO specific therapy can be formally recommended — all drug use is OFF-LABEL
› Treatment goal: reduce NASH-related mortality and prevent progression to cirrhosis or HCC
› Safety and tolerability are prerequisites given significant polypharmacy burden in these patients
★ Recommendation: Pharmacotherapy should be reserved for patients with
NASH, particularly for those with significant fibrosis (stage F2 and higher). Patients B 1
with less severe disease, but at high risk of disease progression could also be evidence rec. grade
candidates for treatment

items.title: Available Agents and Evidence
items.text:
Available Agents and Evidence
• Insulin sensitizers
– Little evidence of histological efficacy with metformin
– PPAR agonist pioglitazone better than placebo
• Improved all histological features except fibrosis
• Achieved resolution of NASH more often
• Antioxidants
– Vitamin E may improve steatosis, inflammation and ballooning and resolve NASH in
some patients
• Concerns about long-term safety exist
★ Recommendation: While no firm recommendations can be made, pioglitazone* or B 2
vitamin E† or their combination could be used for NASH evidence rec. grade
The optimal duration of therapy is unknown; in patients with increased ALT at
baseline, treatment should be stopped if there is no reduction in aminotransferases C 2
after 6 months of therapy
• Lipid-lowering agents
– Statins have not been adequately tested in NASH
★ Recommendation: Statins may be confidently used to reduce LDL cholesterol and
prevent cardiovascular risk, with no benefits or harm to liver disease. B 1
Similarly, n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids reduce both plasma and liver lipids, but evidence rec. grade
there are no data to support their use specifically for NASH
MOA of pharmacological treatments for NAFLD

items.title: Paediatric NAFLD
items.text:
Paediatric NAFLD
• Diet and exercise training reduce steatosis, but do not affect ballooning, inflammation,
and fibrosis
• The long-term outcome of paediatric NASH remains poor
– Drugs have shown beneficial effects but fibrotic lesions are refractory to treatment
★ Recommendation: Diet and physical activity improve steatosis and hepatic
inflammation in paediatric NAFLD, but no beneficial effects on fibrosis have ever been B 1
demonstrated. No safe drug treatment has proven effective on fibrosis in evidence rec. grade
paediatric NAFLD
7.3 Surgical Treatment
A. Bariatric Surgery
• Indicated in patients UNRESPONSIVE to lifestyle changes and pharmacotherapy
• Significantly reduces weight and metabolic complications
• Prospective data show improvement in ALL histological lesions of NASH, including fibrosis
• Results are stable in the long term
★ Recommendation: Bariatric surgery reduces liver fat and likely reduces NASH
progression. Prospective data show improvement in all NASH histological lesions B 1
evidence rec. grade
including fibrosis
B. Liver Transplantation (LTx)
★ Recommendation: LTx is an accepted procedure in patients with NASH and end-
stage liver disease. Overall survival is comparable to other indications, despite a A 1
higher cardiovascular mortality. Patients with NASH and liver failure and/or HCC evidence rec. grade
are candidates for liver transplantation
